title: The Lake That Killed 1,700 People in One Night

scenes.text: August twenty-first, nineteen eighty-six. A quiet lake in the mountains of Cameroon. By morning, about seventeen hundred people were dead, along with thousands of animals, and most had not a single wound. What kills a whole valley in its sleep?

label: CAMEROON HIGHLANDS
Dotted with crater lakes
scenes.text: Cameroon's highlands are dotted with crater lakes like these. Every week on Oddly Logical Science, we follow the strangest true science to the end. Today: a lake that breathed out.
Northwest Cameroon, a volcanic highland. Lake Nyos fills an old crater.
On a Thursday evening, the villages around it went to sleep.

label: LAKE NYOS, 1986
Photographed after the eruption
scenes.text: Late that evening, the lake erupted. Not with lava or fire, but with gas. A huge burst of carbon dioxide came out of the deep water.
No fire. No lava. Just air that could no longer keep you alive.

label: ILLUSTRATION
The real cloud was invisible
scenes.text: Carbon dioxide is heavier than air, so the cloud did not rise. It poured over the crater rim and ran down the valleys, up to about twenty-five kilometers away. The real cloud was invisible. These clouds are only an illustration.
Normal air holds about four hundredths of one percent carbon dioxide. At around ten percent, people can pass out within minutes. Most victims never woke up.
scenes.fact: Carbon dioxide has no color and no smell.\NYou cannot see it, so you cannot flee it.

scenes.caption: PEOPLE DIED OVERNIGHT, UP TO 25 KM FROM THE LAKE
scenes.text: By morning, about seventeen hundred people were dead, along with some three thousand five hundred cattle. The nearest village, Lower Nyos, was almost wiped out. A few survivors lay unconscious for many hours before they woke up, and found everyone around them gone.

label: CAMEROON
Seen from space
scenes.text: If you want true stories this strange, subscribe to Oddly Logical Science. Because the morning after was even more shocking.
Survivors walked down at dawn into total silence. They found whole families dead in their homes, and cattle lying in the fields, without a wound on them.
News took time to reach the outside world. Rumors spread fast: a volcano, a bomb, a secret weapon. Some survivors had strange skin lesions. No one knew what had really happened.
scenes.fact: Skin lesions on survivors are real, but\Ntheir exact cause is still debated.

scenes.text: Within days, scientists from around the world arrived.

The clues pointed away from a bomb or a volcano: no fire, no ash, no blast. Most of the dead had no wounds, and the plants around them were unharmed. And the lake itself had changed. Its water, once blue, had turned a rusty red-brown.
The level had dropped by about a meter, and plants along the shore were flattened. Samples pointed to one suspect: carbon dioxide, dissolved in huge amounts in the deep water.

label: LAKE MONOUN
August 1984
scenes.text: And it had happened before. In August 1984, thirty-seven people died near Lake Monoun, about a hundred kilometers away. Now the pattern was clear.
scenes.fact: Scientists call it a LIMNIC ERUPTION. Only\Na few lakes are known to be capable of it.

scenes.text: The trigger is still debated: a landslide, cold rain, or a volcanic event. Nobody knows.

scenes.question: Where was the carbon dioxide hiding?
options: In the air above the lake
In a cave under the village
scenes.text: So where was all that carbon dioxide hiding, before it erupted?

scenes.heading: INSIDE THE LAKE
scenes.yt_chapter: The science: a lake like a soda bottle
scenes.text: It was hiding in the lake itself. Deep under Nyos, volcanic carbon dioxide seeps into the bottom water. The lake is layered: light water on top, cold dense water below, and the two barely mix. For years, the deep layer quietly filled with gas.

scenes.heading: WHY IT NEVER LEAKED
scenes.text: The crater formed in a volcanic explosion roughly four hundred years ago. In most lakes, the seasons stir the water, and any gas leaks out harmlessly. But Nyos sits in a deep, sheltered crater, with a warm, steady climate and little seasonal change. Nothing stirred it, so the gas piled up for years.
Think of a sealed soda bottle. Under pressure, the gas stays dissolved. Open it, and the gas rushes out.

scenes.heading: A GIANT SODA BOTTLE
scenes.text: At the bottom of Nyos, the pressure is roughly twenty times what we feel at the surface. The lake was a giant bottle, with a hidden cap of cold, dense water holding the gas in. Then something opened it.

scenes.heading: THE CHAIN REACTION

elements.text: MORE GAS... NO WAY TO STOP IT

scenes.text: Once deep water is pushed upward, the pressure drops and the gas forms bubbles. Bubbles make the water lighter, so it rises faster, releasing even more gas. A chain reaction, and nothing could stop it. In a matter of minutes, a vast amount of gas surged to the surface.
scenes.fact: Published estimates: roughly 0.3 to 1.6\Ncubic kilometers of CO2 were released.

label: LAKE NYOS
Degassing, 2000s
scenes.text: After 1986, the fear was simple: the gas was building up again. So in 2001, a team including French researcher Michel Halbwachs installed a pipe in Lake Nyos.

scenes.heading: THE DEGASSING PIPE

elements.text: GAS BUBBLES OUT AS WATER RISES
CO2 LEAVES A LITTLE AT A TIME

scenes.text: The pipe reaches the deep water. Once the flow starts, gas-rich water rises by itself, bubbling out as it climbs, with no pump needed. The lake is opened slowly, like a soda bottle, instead of all at once. At Nyos you can see it working: gas-rich water shoots up from the pipe as a fountain, day after day, quietly emptying the lake of its danger.

scenes.heading: FROM DISASTER TO DEGASSING
scenes.text: Monoun got its pipe in 2003. In 2011, two more pipes were added at Nyos, and reports say the danger has dropped a lot, though monitoring continues.

label: LAKE KIVU
Rwanda and Congo
scenes.text: But Nyos is not the only lake like this. On the border of Rwanda and Congo, Lake Kivu is far bigger, nearly five hundred meters deep, and holds hundreds of cubic kilometers of dissolved gas, mostly carbon dioxide and methane. About two million people live along its shores, in cities like Goma in Congo and Gisenyi in Rwanda.
scenes.fact: Kivu: roughly 2 million people nearby,\Nroughly 250 km³ of CO2 (rough estimate).

scenes.text: Compared with Nyos, Kivu holds hundreds of times more gas. The good news: for its depth, that gas is far from the saturation point, so scientists consider a sudden eruption unlikely any time soon. The bad news: it sits in one of Africa's most active volcanic regions. Researchers monitor its gas levels closely.

So the lake is watched closely. The volcano Nyiragongo, beside Goma, erupted in 2002 and again in 2021. And in Rwanda, power plants now pull the methane out of Kivu to make electricity, which also removes some of the gas from the lake.
So what killed seventeen hundred people in their sleep? Not a monster. Not a weapon.

A lake that stored a deadly gas for years, silently, until the night it breathed out. This time, we know how to listen. Would you have heard it coming? Tell me in the comments. And if this story stayed with you, watch another one on this channel now.

youtube.title: The Lake That Killed 1,700 People in One Night
youtube.description:
On the night of August 21, 1986, Lake Nyos in Cameroon released a huge cloud of carbon dioxide that killed about 1,700 people and some 3,500 cattle in their sleep. How does a lake do that, and could it happen again?

In this video:
- The night Lake Nyos erupted
- The morning after
- The mystery: Monoun, 1984, and the trigger
- The science: a lake like a soda bottle
- Could it happen again? Degassing pipes and Lake Kivu

FAQ
What is a limnic eruption? A sudden release of dissolved gas, mostly CO2, from a deep lake.
Why did people die? Carbon dioxide is heavier than air, flowed into villages and displaced breathable air.
What triggered Nyos? Unproven: a landslide, cold rain or wind, or a small volcanic event are the main candidates.
Can it happen again? Pipes now release gas at Nyos and Monoun. Kivu holds far more gas but is considered much less primed.

Would you have heard it coming? Tell me in the comments.

Sources: Kling et al. 1987, Science 236; Sigvaldason 1989; Kling et al. 2005, PNAS; Schmid et al. 2005, Geochem. Geophys. Geosyst.; USGS Volcano Hazards Program.
